concerns.text: The 'Citation Isolation' metric is defined as 'Degree centrality of nodes with no external incoming edges.' This definition is mathematically contradictory. Degree centrality measures the number of connections a node has; a node with 'no external incoming edges' has an in-degree of zero. If the metric is simply the count of such nodes, it is a 'count of isolated nodes,' not a 'degree centrality.' If it is a centrality score, it cannot be applied to nodes with zero edges. This construct validity failure means the metric cannot measure 'hallucination' as intended.

The plan proposes a permutation test to verify significance but does not specify the number of permutations (marked '[deferred]'). For a p-value threshold of 0.05, a minimum of 1,000 permutations is required to achieve a standard error of ~0.007. With a 6-hour CPU limit and NLP-heavy graph construction, the number of permutations may be severely constrained. Without a defined minimum permutation count or a power analysis, the study risks being underpowered to detect the effect, rendering the significance test invalid.

The 'Semantic Distance' metric is defined as 'Mean pairwise cosine distance... within the same graph component.' This construct is ambiguous for disconnected graphs. If a graph has multiple components, does the metric average across all pairs in the entire graph (ignoring connectivity) or only within components? If the latter, how are components with single nodes handled (distance is undefined)? This ambiguity prevents the metric from reliably measuring 'semantic coherence' or 'hallucination'.
